paper.title: Space-Adiabatic Perturbation Theory
paper.abstract:
We study approximate solutions to the Schr\"odinger equation
$i\epsi\partial\psi_t(x)/\partial t = H(x,-i\epsi\nabla_x) \psi_t(x)$ with the
Hamiltonian given as the Weyl quantization of the symbol $H(q,p)$ taking values
in the space of bounded operators on the Hilbert space $\Hi_{\rm f}$ of fast
``internal'' degrees of freedom. By assumption $H(q,p)$ has an isolated energy
band. Using a method of Nenciu and Sordoni \cite{NS} we prove that interband
transitions are suppressed to any order in $\epsi$. As a consequence,
associated to that energy band there exists a subspace of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\Hi
_{\rm f})$ almost invariant under the unitary time evolution. We develop a
systematic perturbation scheme for the computation of effective Hamiltonians
which govern approximately the intraband time evolution. As examples for the
general perturbation scheme we discuss the Dirac and Born-Oppenheimer type
Hamiltonians and we reconsider also the time-adiabatic theory.

statements.name: Theorem 2.1
statements.body: \hspace{-5pt} Assume either\hspace{-1pt} (IG)$_{m}$\hspace{-1pt} or \hspace{-1pt}(CG). Let $\widehat{H}$ be the Weyl quantization of $H$. Then there exists an orthogonal projector $\Pi \in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} )$ such that \begin{equation} \big[\,\widehat{H},\,\Pi\, \big]=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty }) \end{equation} and $\Pi =\widehat{\pi}+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty })$, where $\widehat{\pi}$ is the Weyl quantization of a semiclassical symbol \[ \pi \asymp \sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}\pi_{j}\qquad \mbox{in }S_{\rho }^{0}(\varepsilon ) \] whose principal part $\pi_{0}(z)$ is the spectral projector of $H_{0}(z)$ corresponding to ${\sigma_{\rm r}}(z)$.
statements.slogan: Under certain conditions, there exists an approximate projection operator that almost commutes with the quantized Hamiltonian, and this projection is close to the quantization of a classical symbol whose leading term projects onto a selected part of the Hamiltonian's spectrum. The error in both the commutation and the approximation is extremely small, decreasing faster than any power of the small parameter epsilon. This result connects classical and quantum projections in a semiclassical setting.

statements.name: Remark 2.2
statements.body: \em Note that the growth condition on the gap in (IG)$_m$ is stronger than one would expect from the analysis in \cite{NS} or \cite{general}. Indeed, in both examples a gap which is bounded globally over phase space suffices to prove uniform adiabatic decoupling also in the presence of a Hamiltonian with principal symbol increasing linearly in momentum. More general, uniform adiabatic decoupling should hold whenever (IG)$_m$ is satisfied with $\gamma = m-\rho$. Indeed (\ref{TIScom}) follows from the following proof with slight modifications under this weaker condition on the growth of the gap. However, this modified proof does not give $\pi\in S^0_\rho(\varepsilon)$, a fact we will make use of in the following. To avoid further complications in the presentation, we decided to state only the stronger result for the stronger growth condition.
statements.slogan: The condition on the size of the energy gap needed for uniform adiabatic decoupling is stronger than what might be expected, as a smaller, globally bounded gap could suffice in some cases, but the stronger condition ensures better control over the mathematical properties of the resulting projector.

statements.name: Lemma 2.3
statements.body: Assume either (IG)$_{m}$ or (CG). Then there exists a \emph{unique} formal symbol \[ \pi =\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}\pi_{j}\qquad \pi_{j}\in S_{\rho }^{-j\rho }(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))\,, \] such that $\pi_{0}(z)$ is the spectral projector of $H_{0}(z)$ corresponding to ${\sigma_{\rm r}}(z),$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $\pi\, \#\, \pi =\pi ,$ \item $\pi^{*}=\pi ,$ \item $[\,H,\,\pi\,]_{\#}:= H\, \#\, \pi -\pi\, \#\, H=0.$ \end{enumerate}
statements.slogan: There is a unique formal series pi made of terms involving powers of epsilon, where each term belongs to a specific symbol class, starting with the spectral projector of H0(z) for the given eigenvalue; this series satisfies three conditions: it is idempotent under a product operation, self-adjoint, and commutes with the Hamiltonian H under the same product.

statements.name: Theorem 3.1
statements.body: Assume either (IG)$_{m}$ or (CG) and that there exists a $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}})$-valued map $u_{0}\in S_{\rho }^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ which satisfies (\ref {Intertwining}). Then there exist a unitary operator $U\in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} )$ such that \begin{equation} U \,\Pi\, U^*={\Pi_{\rm r}} \end{equation} and $U=\widehat{u}+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty })$, where $u\asymp\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}u_{j}$ in $S_{\rho }^{0}(\varepsilon )$ with principal symbol $u_{0}$.
statements.slogan: There exists a unitary operator U that transforms Pi into Pi_r, where U is approximately equal to a quantized symbol u, which has an asymptotic expansion in powers of epsilon starting with u0, and the error is smaller than any power of epsilon. The transformation is valid under certain conditions involving (IG)_m or (CG) and a specific intertwining property. The map u0 takes values in unitary operators on a fiber Hilbert space and belongs to a symbol class. The result provides a semiclassical approximation to a unitary equivalence between two operators.

statements.name: Remark 3.2
statements.body: \em In \cite{NS} the Nagy transformation (\ref{Nagy}) is used in order to map Ran$\Pi$ to the $\varepsilon$-independent subspace Ran$\widehat \pi_0$. This is possible because in their application the symbol $\pi_0$ depends only on $q$ and, as a consequence, $\widehat \pi_0$ is a projector satisfying $\|\Pi-\widehat \pi_0\|=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)$. However, in general $\pi_0$ depends on $q$ and $p$, see Section~6 and \cite{PST2} for relevant examples, and the mapping to the reference space becomes more subtle.
statements.slogan: In some applications, the Nagy transformation can map a range of operators to a reference subspace that does not depend on the small parameter ε, because the leading-order symbol depends only on position; however, when the symbol depends on both position and momentum, as in more general cases, this mapping is more complex and requires a more careful approach.

statements.name: Lemma 3.3
statements.body: Assume either (IG)$_{m}$ or (CG) and that there exists a $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}})$-valued map $u_{0}\in S_{\rho }^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ which satisfies (\ref {Intertwining}). Then there is a formal symbol $u=\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}u_{j}$, with $u_{j}\in S_{\rho }^{-j\rho }( \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$, such that \begin{enumerate} \item $u^{*} \#\, u=1\qquad$ and \qquad $u\, \#\, u^{*}=1$\,, \item $u \, \#\,\, \pi\, \#\, u^*=\pi_{\mathrm{r}}$\,, \end{enumerate} \noindent where $\pi$ is the Moyal projector constructed in Lemma \ref{Prop Moyal proj}. \bigskip
statements.slogan: There exists a formal power series u in powers of epsilon, with coefficients in certain symbol classes, such that u is invertible with respect to the Moyal product, its inverse is its adjoint, and it transforms a given projector pi into a reference projector pi_r via conjugation using the Moyal product. This holds under certain assumptions on the initial data and either of two conditions (IG)_m or (CG). The transformation preserves the algebraic properties of the projector under the Moyal product structure. The construction relies on a previously built Moyal projector.

statements.name: Remark 3.4
statements.body: \emph{ We emphasize that -- as opposed to the Moyal projector $\pi$ appearing in Lemma \ref{Prop Moyal proj} -- the Moyal unitary $u$ is highly non-unique even for fixed $u_0$. As it will follow from the proof, all the possible choices of Moyal unitaries intertwining $\pi$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{r}}$ with prescribed principal symbol $u_0$ are parametrized by the antihermitian Moyal symbols which are diagonal in the $\pi_{\mathrm{r}}$-splitting.}\bigskip
statements.slogan: The Moyal unitary u is not unique even when u0 is fixed, and all possible choices of such unitaries that connect pi and pir with a given principal symbol u0 are determined by antihermitian Moyal symbols that are diagonal in the pir-splitting.

statements.name: Remark 3.5
statements.body: \emph{We sketch how to prove the existence of a smooth map $u_{0}$ satisfying (\ref{Intertwining}). Given \[ E=\left\{ (z,\psi )\in \mathbb{R}^{2d}\times \mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}:\psi \in \mathrm{Ran}\pi_0 (z)\right\} \] the map $\Pi_{E}:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2d},$ \ $(z,\psi )\mapsto z$ defines a fibration of Hilbert spaces over the base space $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$. } \emph{The fibration is locally trivial. Indeed for any $z_{0}\in \mathbb{R}^{2d} $ there exists a neighborhood $\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}$ such that $\left\| \pi _{0}(z)-\pi_{0}(z_{0})\right\| <1$ for any $z\in \mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}$, so that the Nagy formula \[ w(z)=\left[ 1-\left( \pi_{0}(z)-\pi_{0}(z_{0})\right)^{2}\right]^{-\frac{ 1}{2}}\left[ \pi_{0}(z)\pi_{0}(z_{0})+(1-\pi_{0}(z))(1-\pi _{0}(z_{0}))\right] \] locally defines a unitary operator $w(z)$ such that $w(z)^{*}\pi_{0}(z) w(z)=\pi_{0}(z_{0})$. A local trivialization of the fibration is then explicitly given by \[ \begin{array}{cccccc} \Theta : & \Pi_{E}^{-1}(\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}) & \rightarrow & \mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}\times \mathrm{Ran}\pi (z_{0}) & \rightarrow & \mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}\times \mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & (z,\psi ) & \mapsto & (z,w(z)\psi ) & \mapsto & (z,\phi (z_{0})w(z)\psi ) \end{array} \] where we use the fact that there exists a unitary operator $\phi (z_{0}):\mathrm{Ran}\pi (z_{0})\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}$. The existence of $\phi (z_{0})$ follows from the fact that the dimension of $\mathrm{Ran}\pi (z_{0})$ is independent of $z_{0}$, but the map $z_{0}\mapsto \phi (z_{0})$ may be \textit{a priori} even discontinuous. } \emph{\noindent Moreover one can check that any two such trivializations are $\mathcal{U(K}_{\mathrm{f}})$-compatible, and the previous data define a linear $\mathcal{U(K}_{\mathrm{f}})$-bundle. } \emph{Since the base space is contractible, the bundle is trivial and the associated principal $\mathcal{U(K}_{\mathrm{f}})$-bundle (i.e. the bundle of the orthonormal frames) admits a global \emph{smooth} section. This implies the existence of a \emph{smooth} map $u_{0}:$ $\mathbb{R}^{2d}\rightarrow \mathcal{U(H}_{\mathrm{f}})$ such that (\ref{Intertwining}) holds true.}
statements.slogan: There exists a smooth map u0 from 2d-dimensional real space to the group of unitary operators on a Hilbert space, such that a certain intertwining condition holds, because the underlying fiber bundle over a contractible base space is trivial and admits a smooth global section.

statements.name: Theorem 4.1
statements.body: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{Th unitaries}, one has that $h\in S^m_\rho(\varepsilon)$ and $\widehat h$ is essentially self-adjoint on $\mathcal S$. Furthermore \begin{equation} [\,\widehat{h},\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}\,]=0\,, \end{equation} \begin{equation} e^{-i\widehat H t} - \widehat u^{\,*}\,e^{-i\widehat h t}\,\widehat u = \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon^\infty|t|) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} e^{-i\widehat H t} - U^*\,e^{-i\widehat h t}\,U = \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon^\infty(1+|t|))\,. \end{equation}
statements.slogan: Under certain conditions, an effective Hamiltonian h exists in a specific symbol class and its quantization is essentially self-adjoint, while commuting with a projection operator; the time evolution generated by the original Hamiltonian closely matches that of the effective Hamiltonian up to very small error terms in epsilon for long times.

statements.name: Remark 4.2
statements.body: \em It might seem more natural to define the effective Hamiltonian as \[ H_{\rm eff} = U\,\Pi\,\widehat H\,\Pi\,U^* + U\,({\bf 1}-\Pi)\,\widehat H\,({\bf 1}-\Pi)\,U^*\,. \] Clearly one should have $H_{\rm eff} - \widehat h = \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^\infty)$ in some sense. However, if $\widehat H$ is unbounded, this closeness does not follow in the norm of bounded operators from our results, since $U$ need not be a semiclassical operator. As a consequence no asymptotic expansion of $H_{\rm eff}$ in the norm of bounded operators would be available.
statements.slogan: The proposed definition of the effective Hamiltonian involves projecting the full Hamiltonian onto slow and fast degrees of freedom using a unitary transformation, but if the Hamiltonian is unbounded, this definition does not guarantee a close approximation in the norm of bounded operators, and thus prevents a full asymptotic expansion.

statements.name: Remark 4.3
statements.body: \emph{Note that in the case of ${\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\}$, not only the principal symbol $h_{0}(q,p)={E_{\rm r}}(q,p){\bf 1}_{\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}}$, but also the subprincipal symbol $h_{1}(q,p)$ as given by (\ref{h1d}) is well defined regardless of the gap condition, provided that the spectral projection $\pi_0(q,p)$ is sufficiently regular. Indeed, it can be shown, at least in some special cases, that there is still adiabatic decoupling to leading order and an effective dynamics generated by $\widehat{h}_{0}+\varepsilon \,\widehat{h}_{1}$ without a gap condition \cite{general}, \cite{note}.}
statements.slogan: In some cases, even without a spectral gap, the principal and subprincipal symbols can still be defined and lead to an effective dynamics described by a combination of these symbols, provided the spectral projection is smooth enough. This means approximate decoupling and a simplified evolution equation can hold to leading order. The result applies at least in certain special cases. No gap condition is required for this behavior.

statements.name: Theorem 4.4
statements.body: Let $H(t)$ and ${\sigma_{\rm r}}(t)$ be as above. \begin{enumerate} \item {\rm Decoupled subspace.} There exists a family of orthogonal projectors $\Pi(t)$ such that $\Pi(\cdot)\in S^0(\varepsilon , \mathcal{B(H)})$, $\Pi(t)-\pi_0(t) = \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon)$ and \begin{equation} U(t,s)^*\,\Pi(t)\,U(t,s) = \Pi(s) + \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon^\infty|t-s|)\ \end{equation} uniformly for $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$. Whenever $\partial_t^\alpha H(t)=0$ for some $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and all $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}$, then $\Pi(t) = \pi_0(t)$. \item {\rm Intertwining unitaries.} \hspace{-1.7pt} There exists a family of unitaries $u_0(\cdot)\in C^\infty_{\rm b}(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B(H)})$ with $u_0(t)\,\pi_0(t)\,u_0^*(t) = \pi_0(0) =: \pi_{\rm r}$ and a family of unitaries $\mathcal{U}(\cdot) \in S^0(\varepsilon, \mathcal{B(H)})$ such that \[ \mathcal{U}(t) \,\Pi(t)\, \mathcal{U}^*(t) = \pi_{\rm r} \quad \mbox{and}\quad \mathcal{U}(t) - u_0(t) = \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon) \,. \] \item {\rm Effective dynamics.} There exists a family of self-adjoint operators $h(t)$, $h(\cdot)\in S^0(\varepsilon, \mathcal{B(H)})$, such that \begin{equation} [\, h(t),\, \pi_{\rm r}\,] = 0\qquad \mbox{for all}\qquad t\in\mathbb{R} \end{equation} and the solution of the initial value problem \[ i\varepsilon \partial_{t}U_{\rm eff}(t,s)=h(t)U_{\rm eff} (t,s)\,,\qquad s\in \mathbb{R}\,,\qquad U_{\rm eff}(t,t) = {\bf 1}_{\mathcal{H} } \] satisfies \begin{equation} U(t,s) = \mathcal{U}^*(t) \,U_{\rm eff}(t,s)\, \mathcal{U}(s) + \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon^\infty|t-s|)\,. \end{equation} The asymptotic expansion of $h(t)$ in $\mathcal{B(H)}$ reads \begin{eqnarray} h(t) &\asymp& \sum_{n=0}^\infty\varepsilon^n \left(\sum_{j+k+l=n} u_j(t)\,H_k(t)\,u_l^*(t)\right.\\&&\left. \qquad+\, \frac{i}{2}\sum_{j+k+1=n} \left( u_j(t)\,\dot u_k^*(t) - \dot u_j(t)\,u_k^*(t) \right)\right)\,,\nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $\sum_n\varepsilon^n H_n(t)$ is the asymptotic expansion of $H(t)$ in $\mathcal{B(H)}$ and $\sum_n \varepsilon^n u_n$ is the asymptotic expansion of $\mathcal{U}(t)$ in $\mathcal{B(H)}$. \end{enumerate}
statements.slogan: There exists a slowly varying projection onto a subspace that stays approximately invariant under the evolution of a time-dependent quantum system, and the system's dynamics can be approximated by an effective Hamiltonian acting within this subspace, up to errors that are extremely small for small values of the adiabatic parameter. A family of unitary transformations aligns this evolving subspace with a fixed reference subspace, and the effective dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian that commutes with the projection onto this fixed subspace. The effective Hamiltonian is constructed through an asymptotic expansion involving the original Hamiltonian and the unitary transformations. These results hold uniformly in time and provide a rigorous foundation for adiabatic approximations in quantum mechanics.

statements.name: Theorem 5.1
statements.body: \, Let $H$ satisfy either (IG)$_{m}$ for $m\leq 1$ and $\rho=1$ or (CG) with $\rho=0$. Let ${\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\}$ be an eigenvalue of $H_{0}(q,p)$ of finite multiplicity $\ell$. \noindent Then the classical flow $\Phi^{t}$ generated by ${E_{\rm r}}(q,p)$ and the solution of (\ref{Deq}) with initial condition $D(q,p,0)=\mathbf{1}$ exist globally in time. For $a_{0}\in S_\rho^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}^{\ell}))$, $a_{0}(t)$ given by (\ref{A0}) is a solution of (\ref{Eg1}) and $a_{0}(t)\in S_\rho^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}^{\ell}))$ for all $t$. \noindent For each $T<\infty $ there is a constant $C_{T}<\infty $ such that for all $t\in [-T,T]$ \begin{equation} \left\| a(t)\,-\,\mathcal{W}_\varepsilon\left(a_{0}(t)\right)\right\| \,\leq \,\varepsilon \,C_{T}\,, \end{equation} where $a(t)=e^{i\widehat{h}t/\varepsilon }\,\widehat{a}_{0}\,e^{-i\widehat{h}t/\varepsilon }$.
statements.slogan: Under certain conditions on the Hamiltonian H and its eigenvalues, the classical flow and a specific solution to a differential equation exist for all time. The time evolution of a symbol a0 in a particular class remains in that class, and the difference between the quantum evolution of an observable and its semiclassical approximation is bounded by a constant times the small parameter epsilon, uniformly over finite time intervals.

statements.name: Corollary 5.2
statements.body: Let $H$ satisfy either (IG)$_{m}$ with $m\leq 1$ and $\rho =1$ or (CG) with $\rho=0$ and let ${\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\}$ consist of a single eigenvalue of $H_{0}(q,p)$ of finite multiplicity $\ell$. Let $b_{0}\in S_{1}^{0} (\mathcal{B(H}_{\mathrm{f}}))$ such that $[b_{0},\pi_{0}]=0$ and $B(t):=e^{i\widehat{H}t/\varepsilon }\,\widehat{b}_{0}\,e^{-i\widehat{H}t/\varepsilon }$. Let $a_{0}:=\pi_{\mathrm{r}}\,u_{0}\,b_{0}\,u_{0}^{*}\,\pi_{\mathrm{r}}$ and define $a_{0}(t)$ is in (\ref{A0}). Then for each $T<\infty $ there is a constant $C_{T}<\infty$ such that for all $t\in [-T,T]$ \begin{equation} \left\|\big( B(t)\,-\,\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon }(u_{0}^{*}\,a_{0}(t)\,u_{0})\big)\Pi \right\| \,\leq \,\varepsilon \,C_{T}\,. \end{equation} For $b_{0}=f\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}}$, with $f\in S_{1}^{0}(\mathbb{R})$, one obtains as a special case of (\ref{Eg2}) that \[ \left\|\big( B(t)\,-\,\widehat{b_{0}(\Phi^{t})}\big)\Pi \right\| \,\leq \,\varepsilon \,C_{T}\,. \]
statements.slogan: For a quantum system with an isolated energy band, the time evolution of certain observables is approximately given by a classical evolution up to small errors proportional to the small parameter epsilon, uniformly over finite time intervals. This holds when the system's Hamiltonian has specific regularity and spectral properties. The approximation improves as epsilon becomes smaller. In particular, transitions between different energy bands are strongly suppressed.

statements.name: Theorem 6.1
statements.body: Let $A\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{\infty }(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and ${\phi}\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{\infty }(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R})$. Then there exist orthogonal projectors $\Pi_{\pm }$ with $\Pi_{+}+\Pi_{-}=\mathbf{1}$ such that $[\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}},\Pi_{\pm }]=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty })$, and there exists a unitary $U$ and $\widehat h\in {\rm OP}S^1_1$ with \begin{equation} \widehat h = \left( \begin{array}{cc} \widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}} & 0 \\ 0 & \widehat{h}_{\mathrm{p}} \end{array} \right)\,, \end{equation} such that \begin{equation} e^{-i\widehat H_{\rm D} t} - U^*\,e^{-i\widehat h t}\,U = \mathcal{O}_0(\varepsilon^\infty|t|) \,. \end{equation} Here $\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}}$ and $\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{p}}$ are semiclassical operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{2})$ with \[ h_{\mathrm{ e}}(q,p,\varepsilon )\asymp E_{+}(q,p)\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty }\,\varepsilon^{j}\,h_{\mathrm{e},j}(q,p) \] and $h_{ \mathrm{e},j}=\pi_{\mathrm{r}}(u\,\#\,H_{\mathrm{D}}\,\#\,u^{*})_{j}\pi_{ \mathrm{r}}\in S_{1}^{1-j}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}^{2}))$ for all $j\geq 0$, where $u\in S_{1}^{0}(\varepsilon )$ is constructed as in Section~\ref{SUNI}. In particular, $h_{\mathrm{e,1}}(q,p)$ is given by (\ref{h1D}) and thus \begin{equation} \widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}}=\Big(c\sqrt{m^{2}c^{2}+(-i\varepsilon \hbar \nabla - \frac{e}{c}A(x))^{2}}+e{\phi}(q)\Big)\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}\,-\,\varepsilon \, \frac{\hbar }{2}\,\sigma \cdot \widehat{\Omega (q,p)}\,+\,\mathcal{O}_0 (\varepsilon^{2})\,. \nonumber \end{equation} Analogous results hold for $h_{\mathrm{p}}$. The errors in (\ref{HDexp}) and (\ref{hel}) are in the norm of bounded operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}, \mathbb{C}^{4})$, resp.\ on $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{2})$.\emph{\ }
statements.slogan: For a smooth and bounded magnetic vector potential A and electric potential phi, the time evolution of the Dirac equation can be approximated by decoupling it into two nearly independent parts corresponding to positive and negative energy states, using a unitary transformation and projection operators, with errors smaller than any power of a small parameter epsilon. The effective Hamiltonians for these parts act on two-component wave functions and include relativistic kinetic energy, electromagnetic interactions, and a spin-dependent term correct up to second order in epsilon. Higher-order corrections are systematically defined through an asymptotic expansion. The approximation holds uniformly in time when measured in the operator norm.

statements.name: Definition 8.1
statements.body: A function $A\in C^{\infty }(\mathbb{R}^{2d},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ belongs to the symbol class $S_{\rho }^{m}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{ \mathrm{f}}))$ $($with $m\in \mathbb{R}$ and $0\leq \rho \leq 1)$ if for every $\alpha ,\beta \in \mathbb{N}^{d}$ there exists a positive constant $C_{\alpha ,\beta }$ such that \[ \sup_{q\in \mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\| (\partial_{q}^{\alpha }\partial_{p}^{\beta }A)(q,p)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}})}\leq C_{\alpha ,\beta }\ \left\langle p\right\rangle^{m-\rho |\beta |} \] for every $p\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, where $\left\langle p\right\rangle =(1+|p|^{2})^{1/2}$.
statements.slogan: A smooth function A of position and momentum variables, taking values in bounded operators on a Hilbert space, is in the symbol class S_m^rho if its derivatives in position and momentum grow at most like a power of momentum, specifically with order m minus rho times the number of momentum derivatives, measured in operator norm. The growth bound involves a weight function that behaves like the magnitude of momentum for large values. Each derivative of A is uniformly bounded in position and controlled by this weighted power law in momentum. The constants governing these bounds depend only on the order of the derivatives.

statements.name: Proposition 8.2
statements.body: Let $A\in S^m_\rho(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\rm f}))$, then $\widehat A$ given trough (\ref{Weyl def}) maps $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathcal{H} _{\rm f})$ continuously into itself.
statements.slogan: If A is a symbol in the class S^m_rho with values in bounded operators on a Hilbert space H_f, then the operator A-hat defined by Weyl quantization maps the space of rapidly decreasing smooth functions with values in H_f continuously into itself.

statements.name: Proposition 8.3
statements.body: \emph{(Calderon-Vaillancourt)} There exists a constant $C_{d}<\infty$ such that for every $A\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{2d+1}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ one has \[ \big\| \widehat{A}\big\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} )}\leq C_{d}\sup_{|\alpha |+|\beta |\leq 2d+1}\ \sup_{q,p\in \mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\| (\partial _{q}^{\alpha }\partial_{p}^{\beta }A)(q,p)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}})}=C_{d}\left\| A\right\|_{C_{\mathrm{b}}^{2d+1}}\,. \]
statements.slogan: There is a constant depending only on the dimension d such that the operator norm of the quantized symbol A is bounded by the constant times the supremum of all derivatives of A up to order 2d+1. This applies to symbols that are bounded and sufficiently smooth functions on phase space. The bound ensures that the size of the associated operator is controlled by the smoothness and size of the original function.

statements.name: Proposition 8.4
statements.body: If $A$ $\in S_{\rho }^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ and $B\in S_{\rho }^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$, then $AB$ belongs to\\ $S_{\rho }^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ for every $m_{1},m_{2}\in \mathbb{R}$.\
statements.slogan: If two operators A and B are in symbol classes S_rho^m1 and S_rho^m2 respectively, then their product AB is in the symbol class S_rho^(m1+m2), for any real numbers m1 and m2.

statements.name: Proposition 8.5
statements.body: Assume that $A$ $\in S_{\rho }^{m}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$ is a normal symbol which is elliptic, in the sense that there exists a constant $C_{0}$ such that \[ \rho_{\mathrm{int}}(A(q,p))\geq C_{0}\left\langle p\right\rangle^{m}\qquad \mbox{for any }\,\,p\in \mathbb{R}^{d}\,. \] Then the pointwise inverse $A^{-1}$ exists and belongs to $S_{\rho }^{-m}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H} _{\mathrm{f}}))$.
statements.slogan: If a normal symbol A is elliptic, meaning its internal norm is bounded below by a constant times a power of the momentum variable, then A has a pointwise inverse that is also a symbol of negative order.

statements.name: Proposition 8.6
statements.slogan: If A and B are operators in certain symbol classes with orders m1 and m2, then their composition is another operator whose symbol C is in the symbol class of order m1 + m2, and C is given by a specific oscillatory integral expression involving derivatives of A and B evaluated at the same point.

statements.name: Definition 8.7
statements.body: A map $A:[0,\varepsilon_{0})\rightarrow S_{\rho }^{m},\varepsilon \mapsto A_{\varepsilon }$ is called a semiclassical symbol of order $m$ and weight $ \rho $ if there exists a sequence $\{A_{j}\}_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ with $A_{j}\in S_{\rho }^{m-j\rho }$ such that for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ one has that $ \left( A_{\varepsilon }-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon^{j}A_{j}\right) $ belongs to $S_{\rho }^{m-n\rho }$ {\em uniformly} in $\varepsilon $, in the following sense: for any $k\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists a constant $C_{n,k}$ such that for any $\varepsilon \in [0,\varepsilon_{0})$ one has \begin{equation} \Big\| A_{\varepsilon }-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon^{j}A_{j}\Big\| _{k}^{(m-n\rho )}\leq C_{n,k}\, \varepsilon^{n} \,, \end{equation} where $\left\| \ldots \right\|_{k}^{(m)}$ is the $k$-th Fr\'{e}chet semi-norm in $S_{\rho }^{m},$ introduced in (\ref{Seminorms}).
statements.slogan: A semiclassical symbol of order m and weight rho is a family of functions A_epsilon that can be approximated by a series in powers of epsilon, where each term in the series has a specific decay property, and the error after n terms is bounded by a constant times epsilon to the power n, measured in a certain norm that depends on the order and weight. The approximation holds uniformly for small epsilon. Each term in the series belongs to a class of functions with decreasing regularity and decay. The bound on the error involves seminorms that measure the smoothness and growth of the functions.

statements.name: Proposition 8.8
statements.body: Let be $\{A_{j}\}_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ an arbitrary sequence such that $A_{j}\in S_{\rho }^{m-j\rho }.$ Then there exists $A\in S_{\rho }^{m}(\varepsilon )$ such that $A\asymp \sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}A_{j}$ in $S_{\rho }^{m}(\varepsilon )$ and $A$ is unique up to $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon ^{\infty })$, in the sense that the difference of two such symbols is $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\infty })$ in $S_{\rho }^{m}(\varepsilon )$. The semiclassical symbol $A$ is called a \textbf{resummation} of the formal symbol $\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}A_{j}$.
statements.slogan: There exists a unique semiclassical symbol A, defined up to arbitrarily small errors in powers of a small parameter epsilon, that matches the asymptotic expansion given by a sum of scaled symbols A_j with decreasing regularity and order. This symbol A is called the resummation of the formal series. The result ensures that such asymptotic series can be realized by a genuine symbol in a well-defined function space.

statements.name: Proposition 8.9
statements.body: If $A\asymp \sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}A_{j}$ in $S_{\rho }^{m_{1}}(\varepsilon )$ and $B\asymp \sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}B_{j}$ in $S_{\rho }^{m_{2}}(\varepsilon )$, then $A\ \tilde{\#}\ B\in S_{\rho }^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\varepsilon )$ has an asymptotic expansion given by \begin{equation} \left( A\ \tilde{\#}\ B\right)_{k}(q,p)= (2i)^{-k} \sum_{|\alpha |+|\beta |+j+l=k}\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha |}}{|\alpha |!|\beta |!}\left( (\partial_{q}^{\alpha }\partial_{p}^{\beta }A_{j})(\partial _{p}^{\alpha }\partial_{q}^{\beta }B_{l})\right) (q,p) \end{equation} where it is understood that $k,j,l\in \mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in \mathbb{N}^{d}$.
statements.slogan: If two operators A and B have asymptotic expansions in certain symbol classes parameterized by epsilon, then their composition A tilde sharp B also has an asymptotic expansion in a related symbol class, with each term of the expansion expressed as a finite sum involving derivatives of the terms from the expansions of A and B. The coefficients in this sum depend on combinatorial factors and powers of 2i, and the order of the resulting symbol is the sum of the original orders. The expansion is indexed by the total degree k, which splits into contributions from derivative orders and expansion orders.
